name: Clipboard Check
description: A task completed and officially marked done. The clipboard holds the list, the checkmark seals it. This is what 'finished' looks like when you want someone to know you actually did the thing.
meaning: 📋✅ means a task is complete and verified. The clipboard represents the work itself — the list, the plan, the thing that needed doing. The checkmark transforms it into proof. Together they say 'I had this on my list and I checked it off,' which reads as both accomplished and accountable.
examples: finally organized my entire google drive 📋✅
project brief is approved and ready to go 📋✅
seoDescription: What does 📋✅ mean? It means a task is completed and officially marked done—the clipboard holds the list, the checkmark seals it.

longForm.overview:
📋✅ is the visual equivalent of drawing a line through something. The clipboard is the tangible part — it holds the to-do, the checklist, the responsibilities. The checkmark is the release. What separates this combo from a single ✅ is the clipboard's specificity. A lone checkmark can mean 'approved' or 'yes' or 'got it,' which are lighter reads. Add the clipboard and suddenly you are saying 'I did the work that was on my list.' It is the difference between agreement and completion.

People send 📋✅ when they want credit for finishing something, not just acknowledging it. In group chats it lands after someone has tackled a shared task. In work Slack it shows up when a deliverable is ready or when someone closes out their portion of a project. The combo works because it implies both visibility and follow-through — you had a list, people knew about it, and you finished it.
longForm.howPeopleUseIt:
📋✅ appears in work contexts most often — project completions, task handoffs, approved proposals. It also shows up in personal accountability moments: someone finishes meal prep, cleans their apartment, catches up on emails, and wants to mark it visible. The combo lands in group chats as proof of effort, the kind of message that says 'I said I would do this and here is the evidence.'

It pairs well with short recaps: 'got the budget finalized 📋✅' or 'all vaccinations booked 📋✅.' The sender is not asking for validation so much as announcing that a task has left their plate. In tight friend groups it can read as a small flex — proof that someone actually followed through on what they said they would tackle.
longForm.whenNotToUse:
Skip 📋✅ when you are simply approving someone else's work. A single ✅ reads better as 'looks good' or 'approved.' The clipboard implies you completed the task yourself, not that you verified it. Using the combo to sign off on someone else's work will read as you claiming credit for their effort.

Avoid it in moments that need nuance or softness. If a task is done but the outcome was messy or the person is exhausted, a lone ✅ or a sentence like 'you got it done' lands with more humanity than 📋✅, which can read as clinical or overly formal. In sensitive feedback, skip the combo entirely.
longForm.howToReply:
Mirror 📋✅ if someone sends it to you and you want to celebrate the completion with them. A sentence like 'let's go' or 'nice' paired with 📋✅ reads as you matching their energy. If the completed task was ambitious, a 🙌 or a 😤 adds warmth that the combo alone might miss.

If someone sends you 📋✅ about work you both did, reply with 'we got it 📋✅' to acknowledge the shared effort. If it lands on your own post or message, a simple 'thanks' or 'finally' with a 📋✅ keeps the momentum going without overselling the moment.

faqs.question: What does 📋✅ mean in a group chat?
faqs.answer: It means someone completed a task that the group knew about or cared about. It is proof they followed through, not just a casual 'yes' — it is 'I did the thing on the list.'

faqs.question: Can I use 📋✅ to approve someone else's work?
faqs.answer: No, it reads as you claiming you completed the task. Use a single ✅ or 'approved' if you are signing off on someone else's effort.

faqs.question: Is 📋✅ professional enough for work Slack?
faqs.answer: Yes, it is clear and direct in work contexts. Use it when closing out a task or confirming a deliverable is ready. It reads as efficient, not casual.

faqs.question: What is the difference between 📋✅ and just ✅?
faqs.answer: A single ✅ is lighter — it can mean approval, agreement, or 'got it.' 📋✅ specifically means you completed a task that was on a list or plan.

conversationExamples.message: client contracts all signed and filed 📋✅
conversationExamples.interpretation: Someone completed a multi-step task and is letting their team know it is done and accounted for. Respond with a ✅ or 'great' to acknowledge, or ask if anything else needs to happen next. This is an update, not a request for help.

conversationExamples.message: finally did that deep clean we talked about 📋✅
conversationExamples.interpretation: Your friend followed through on something they mentioned wanting to do and is announcing it to the group. Respond with matching energy like 'let's go 📋✅' or a 'how does it feel' question to celebrate the effort.

conversationExamples.message: booked us a table for saturday 📋✅
conversationExamples.interpretation: Someone took initiative on a plan you both discussed and completed it. This reads as reliability and consideration. Respond with gratitude and maybe a 'excited' emoji to show appreciation for the follow-through.

conversationExamples.message: got all the kids' school forms filled out and turned in 📋✅
conversationExamples.interpretation: A parent or caregiver is checking off a necessary task and wants the family to know it is handled. This is informational and a mild flex on staying organized. Respond with 'thanks' or acknowledgment that one thing is officially off the plate.

conversationExamples.message: just hit publish on the new blog series 📋✅
conversationExamples.interpretation: A creator completed a project they had planned and is announcing it is live. This reads as both proud and professional. Respond by engaging with the content or offering genuine congratulations on shipping it.
